headline: A tech blog puts your build in its Friday roundup.
A streamer with too much time uses your build on camera for an hour.
Your 2am debugging thread does numbers overnight.
DevWorld wants someone from your studio on a panel.
A reviewer spends four paragraphs on your onboarding, none of them kind.
A logging misconfiguration makes the local tech press.
A retired angel wires you money for no reason he'll explain.
Your hosting provider has a very bad Tuesday.
Half the room is coughing. You pay contractors to cover the week.
A letter arrives about a patent on "transmitting data over a network".
body: It is eleven pages of nothing. It is also from real lawyers with real letterhead, and ignoring it has a price.

choices.label: Forward it to a lawyer and forget it
choices.detail: Free if you have Legal · otherwise it drags on

choices.label: File it under "later"
choices.detail: Free now · reputation −2 when it resurfaces

headline: Your laptop makes a noise laptops should not make.
body: The fan gave up somewhere around the third all-nighter. You can replace it today, or you can nurse it and lose hours to crashes.

headline: Your landlord wants the garage back for his cousin's boat.
body: He is apologetic about it in the way people are when they have already decided. The lease is on your side. His cousin is not.

choices.label: Offer him three months up front
Read the lease back to him

headline: The landlord is back, and this time he brought a rent schedule.
Someone you have never met emails to say your thing helped them.
body: No feature request, no bug report. They just wanted you to know. You read it four times.

choices.label: Print it and pin it over your desk

headline: A friend offers you $5,000 for ten percent, over coffee.
body: He sold a logistics company in 2019 and has been bored since. He means it kindly. He will also want to know how it's going, forever.

headline: Your angel wants a call about "the plan".
body: He has read one blog post about your market and has thoughts. Some of them are good. All of them will take an afternoon.

choices.label: Send a two-line update instead
choices.detail: Free · he stops offering to help

headline: A coworking space offers you a free month to leave the garage.
body: Free coffee, a printer, and thirty people who will ask what you're building. After the month it's real money.

choices.label: Stay where the rent is zero

headline: The street loses power for six hours. Nothing was committed.
The domain you actually wanted is for sale.
body: The squatter who has been sitting on it since 2011 has decided this is the year. He is asking $2,300 and will not be negotiating.

headline: A student hackathon wants a judge and offers nothing but pizza.
body: Forty hours of other people's demos. Some of them will be looking for a job in eighteen months.

headline: An accelerator emails a form letter with your company name pasted in.
body: Three months, a demo day, and seven percent. Every founder you know has an opinion about this and none of them agree.

headline: Latency has been creeping up for a week and nobody has said it out loud.
body: The graphs are still green. They are green the way a bridge is standing.

choices.label: Stop the week and fix the infrastructure
Restart it nightly and move on

headline: Everything is down, and it has been down for two hours.
body: Support is a wall of the same screenshot. Somebody on social media is timing you.

headline: You publish the postmortem. It is unflattering and people respect it.
One customer is using ninety percent of your free tier.
body: They are a fourteen-year-old running something ambitious in a country where your prices are absurd. They are also expensive.

choices.label: Comp the account and say so publicly

headline: A stranger emails you a working exploit and a 90-day clock.
body: The email is polite, precise, and correct. There is no bounty programme to pay them from.

choices.label: Pay a bounty and fix it this week
Fix it quietly, thank them by email
choices.detail: Free · they post about it anyway

headline: The store rejects your update over a guideline written in 2016.
body: The reviewer's note is three sentences and contradicts itself once. There is an appeal form.

headline: The store puts you on a shelf called "Quietly Excellent".
Two of your engineers want to open-source an internal tool.
body: It is the scheduler they built in a weekend. It is genuinely good. It is also the only thing you do faster than anyone else.

choices.label: Ship it under your name
choices.detail: Reputation +7 · team morale +8 · rivals get it too

headline: The office wifi drops every time the microwave runs.
A reporter who actually covers this beat wants twenty minutes.
body: She has read your changelog, which nobody does. She wants to know why you started, and she will print whatever you say.

choices.label: Tell her the truth, including the bad parts
choices.detail: Reputation +3 now · the profile lands in three weeks

choices.label: Say you're heads-down
choices.detail: Free · she writes about someone else

headline: The profile runs. It quotes the part where you said you almost quit.
body: Three people email to say they needed to read that today. Two investors email to ask if it's still true.

choices.label: Lean into it — write your own follow-up
Let it stand on its own

headline: The piece runs. It is four paragraphs and one of them is your boilerplate.
The same reporter is writing about founders who overshare.
body: You are the friendly example. She wants to know whether it worked out. She will run the piece either way.

choices.label: Point her at the product instead

headline: A reporter is asking your ex-employees what it was like to work here.
body: She has three on the record and one who will not go on it. You have a week before it runs.

choices.label: Sit down with her
choices.detail: Reputation −2 · morale +5 · it could be worse

choices.label: Send a statement through a PR firm

headline: A conference offers you a keynote slot and no fee.
body: Eight hundred people, forty minutes, and three weeks of writing it in the evenings.

choices.label: Decline
choices.detail: Free · reputation −1, they ask someone else

headline: You are shortlisted for an award nobody in the office has heard of.
body: The ceremony is black tie and the table costs money. The trophy is, apparently, quite heavy.

choices.label: Buy a table and take the team

headline: Someone who left before the company had a name is claiming equity.
body: You remember the whiteboard session. You do not remember promising twenty percent. Neither of you wrote anything down.

choices.label: Hire a lawyer and fight it
choices.detail: −$6,000 · months of it · you probably win

headline: The claim is dismissed. Your lawyer sends a final invoice and a smiley face.
Your ex-cofounder posts a gracious thread about the early days.
Your ex-cofounder writes it all up publicly, with screenshots.
body: The screenshots are real. The framing is not. It is the third-most-read thing on the internet this morning.

choices.label: Settle now, at the worse price

headline: The tax office has questions about your second year.
body: Nothing is alleged. Everything is requested, in triplicate, by the fifteenth.

choices.label: Pay an accountant to handle it
Do it yourself over two weekends

headline: A vendor you use had a breach, and your customer emails were in it.
body: Not your bug. Entirely your problem. Disclosure law starts a clock the moment you know.

headline: The breach makes the trade press, and so does your silence.
A company in another country has your name and got there first.
body: Their product is a brand of shelving. Their lawyers are thorough.

headline: A client's standard contract quietly assigns them your source code.
body: It is on page eleven, in the same font as everything else. Their procurement team says it is non-negotiable, which is what procurement teams say.

headline: A recruiter has been messaging your whole team on the same day.
body: Two of them mentioned it. The rest did not, which is the part worth thinking about.

choices.label: Do a pay review this week

headline: A student asks to intern for free.
body: She is better than her CV. Free is not actually free, and it is also not actually fair.

choices.label: Tell her to come back with a salary line

headline: Someone stayed until 3am three nights running and nobody asked them to.
body: They think this is what commitment looks like. They learned it from watching you.

choices.label: Send them home and mean it

headline: An anonymous review of your company appears, and it is specific.
body: Specific enough that you know roughly who wrote it. Accurate enough that arguing would be worse.

choices.label: Bring it to the team meeting

headline: The team wants an offsite. Not a trust fall — a week somewhere with a whiteboard.
body: Somebody has already found a place with a fireplace and sent the link round. A week away is a week not shipping, and everybody knows it.

headline: Two people booked a meeting room with no meeting in it.
body: There is a group chat you are not in. There has been for a while.

choices.label: Ask them what they want, in writing

headline: They have a list. It is shorter and more reasonable than you feared.
body: Predictable hours, a written promotion ladder, and one number you would rather not pay.

choices.label: Agree to everything but the number

headline: The vote happens. You find out the result from the trade press.
Your best engineer has started fixing things nobody asked about.
body: That is what boredom looks like on someone who cannot sit still. The next stage is a resignation you did not see coming.

choices.label: Give them something hard to own
choices.detail: Their morale +14 · nothing else moves this week

headline: Someone on the team wants to refer a friend, and is nervous about asking.
body: They have worked together before and they are not exaggerating. What they actually want to know is whether asking counts against them.

choices.label: Set a referral bonus and say so publicly

headline: A senior on your team has been teaching the juniors on their own time.
A bigger company suggests coffee, twice, in a way that is not about coffee.
body: Their corp-dev lead has a spreadsheet with your name in it. Coffee is how this always starts.

headline: Diligence begins. They want four years of everything by Friday.
body: Two of your engineers are now full-time on a data room. Nobody is building anything.

choices.label: Give them everything
choices.detail: −$5,000 · nothing ships · they make an offer

headline: The offer arrives. It is real, and it is lower than the coffee implied.
body: There is a two-year earn-out with a performance gate you would not have agreed to sober. Their corp-dev lead calls it "standard".

choices.label: Counter, hard
choices.detail: Reputation +4 · they respect it or they don't

choices.label: Walk, and tell the team why

headline: Corp-dev goes quiet. Someone else announces an acquisition in your space two weeks later.
Someone offers to introduce you to a fund, unprompted.
body: The introduction is free. The meeting is two days of preparation you do not have.

choices.label: Prepare properly and take the meeting
Ask for it after the next launch
choices.detail: Free · you keep the two days

headline: Your bank would like a word about the loan.
body: Nothing is overdue. They are checking, in the way that means someone flagged the account.

headline: A regional innovation grant is open. The form is forty pages.
body: The money is real and so is the weekend it costs. Roughly one application in three gets anything at all.

headline: A client is ninety days late and has stopped replying to invoices.
body: Their office phone rings out. Their marketing account posts twice a day.

choices.label: Write it off and stop working for them

headline: Your business insurance renews at double, citing "sector risk".
body: Nothing has changed at your end. The broker says everyone in software got the same letter, and says it like that settles it.

headline: Your accountant found something you have been paying for since year one.
A pipe upstairs decides to become everyone's problem at 4am.
The coffee machine has died and the team is treating it as a bereavement.
body: There is a printed note taped to it. Three people have already looked up replacements and sent you the expensive one.

headline: The startup next door has installed a gong for closed deals.
body: They are closing a lot of deals. It comes through the wall at roughly ninety-minute intervals, and it is a good gong.

headline: Facilities wants to know what goes on the sign above reception.
body: It is the first thing every candidate and every journalist will see. Facilities need an answer by Friday to get it made.

choices.label: The logo, lit, six feet tall
The company name, small, in a decent typeface

headline: A competitor ships your best feature, badly, with a better landing page.
body: The screenshots are close enough to be a compliment and far enough to be legal.

choices.label: Ship the next three things faster

headline: Your pricing page changed and three hundred people noticed.
body: The loudest of them has been a customer since the beginning and is not wrong.

choices.label: Grandfather everyone who was already paying

headline: The platform announces an API change that breaks a third of your product.
An analyst firm puts you in a quadrant and offers to explain it for a fee.
body: You are in the bottom left. The briefing will not move you, but the people who read these reports notice who turns up.

headline: Every second app on the front page is suddenly about running.
A high-profile launch goes badly and takes the whole category's goodwill with it.
A large customer's procurement team sends a 200-question security review.
body: Question 84 asks which data centre you operate. You do not operate a data centre. The contract at the end of it is the biggest you have been offered.

choices.label: Tell them you're not enterprise-ready yet

headline: The big industry conference has one booth left and a deadline of Friday.
body: Everyone you compete with will be there. A booth buys you the room; the hallway is free and about half as good.

choices.label: Go without a booth and work the hallway

headline: A nonprofit wants your software free, forever, for a good reason.
body: They are small, they are serious, and they will use it properly. “Free forever” is a support cost with no invoice attached.

choices.label: Give it to them and say nothing publicly
Give it to them and put out a press release

headline: Your old manager calls to offer you your job back, with a title.
body: The number is more than you have paid yourself all year. He is not being unkind; he genuinely thinks he is helping.

choices.label: Say you'll think about it
choices.detail: Mood −6 · you think about it for a month

headline: A founder dinner invitation arrives. Twelve people, one long table, no phones.
body: You would know two of the twelve. It is the kind of evening that is either the best thing this month or four hours you do not get back.

headline: Someone respected offers to advise you for a small slice.
body: You have seen their name on three companies you admire. You have also seen it on eleven you have not heard of.

headline: An auditor asks whether you would like to explain the Q3 reversal over lunch.
body: They are being extremely pleasant about it, which is how you know.

choices.label: Go to the lunch
choices.detail: Reputation +1 · they leave with a photocopy

headline: Somebody has ordered a second shredder.
body: Nobody will say who. The invoice is under 'office supplies'.

headline: A resignation letter arrives with four attachments.
body: The letter is one paragraph. The attachments are not.

choices.label: Do nothing at all
choices.detail: Free · and it stays out there

headline: A reporter you have never met asks about a payment you have never mentioned.
body: They have the amount right to the dollar, which narrows it down considerably.

choices.label: Give them a statement
choices.detail: Reputation −2 · it is a small story

choices.label: No comment
choices.detail: Reputation −5 · it is a bigger one

headline: A law firm sends an unsolicited retainer proposal.
body: The covering letter says they have been 'following your growth with interest'.

headline: Your finance lead asks, in writing, for the Q2 file to be corrected.
body: In writing is the part that matters. In writing is always the part that matters.

choices.label: Tell them it's fine
choices.detail: Morale −6 · and they keep the email

headline: An anonymous post about your studio has 400 replies.
body: Two of the replies are extremely specific. One of them is from your building.

headline: Your directors' liability insurance comes up for renewal at three times the price.
body: The broker calls it 'a market-wide adjustment' and will not meet your eye on video.

headline: An investor's diligence team asks for the last eight quarters, unaudited.
body: Unaudited is what they asked for. Unaudited is what worries you.

headline: Somebody asks, in the all-hands, whether the rumours are true.
body: The room is very quiet and forty people are looking at the same place.

choices.label: Tell them what you can
choices.detail: Morale +5 · and it is out of the room

headline: Your bank moves the account to 'enhanced monitoring'.
body: Nothing changes except that everything takes four working days.

headline: A crisis PR firm pitches you before there is a crisis.
body: 'We like to be early,' they say, which is not reassuring from a crisis firm.

choices.label: Pass
choices.detail: Free · you will handle it yourself

headline: A rival founder is asked about you on stage and takes their time answering.
body: 'I'd rather build than comment,' they say, having commented.

headline: Two people arrive with a box and a list of what goes in it.
body: They are polite, they are quick, and they take the good laptop.

headline: Somebody breaches the gag order on a podcast.
body: It was not you, and it will be treated as though it was.

headline: HR suggests, gently, that you might want a compliance officer.
body: They have already written the job description. It is two pages.

headline: A customer's legal team writes about a feature they were shown and never got.
body: They have the recording of the demo. Of course they have the recording.

headline: A former employee is writing a book about a start-up that is obviously yours.
body: The working title is a phrase you said in a meeting.

headline: A regulator sends a letter that asks eleven questions and answers none.
body: Question seven is about a week you would rather not think about.

headline: The rumour that the office was searched is now a rumour that it is being searched.
body: It is not. Three people have gone home anyway.

headline: A supplier quietly moves you to payment in advance.
body: Their account manager calls it 'a routine review of terms'. It is not routine.

headline: A conference that invited you to keynote has 'restructured the programme'.
body: The new programme has a panel where your talk was, and you are not on it.
